vignette:
She sits on the floor of the master bedroom, a tangle of copper wires spread across the drop cloth. The house is quiet—the owners are at work—and she prefers it that way. At fifty-four, her hands are steady, her eyes still sharp enough to read the color bands on resistors without glasses. But there is a new tremor in her left hand that appears only when she stops moving. She flexes her fingers, waits for it to pass, and picks up the wire strippers.

Eighteen months ago, she was not on her knees in a stranger’s house. She was on her back in a hospital bed, staring at a ceiling tile that had a hairline crack shaped like a river. She remembers counting the tributaries. The diagnosis had come six weeks earlier—stage two breast cancer, aggressive, triple-negative. The surgeon had been matter-of-fact: “We’ll start with chemo, then surgery, then radiation.” She had nodded as if he were describing a wiring diagram. She was good at following steps.

But the steps led to a place she could not have mapped. The chemo felt like a slow electrocution, wave after wave of nausea and bone pain. She lost her hair, her appetite, her sense of smell. Then came the fever that would not break—the sepsis that nearly finished what the cancer had started. She remembers the doctor’s face swimming above her, his mouth moving, and the word “unstable” landing like a heavy tool in her chest. For the first time since childhood, she had prayed. Not to any god she knew. Just a raw, silent plea for one more day of breath.

She got the breath. The cancer is gone now. The hair has grown back, gray and thin. She returned to work eight months ago, because the bills never stopped, and the divorce had already taken half of everything. Her ex-husband had left during the treatment. “I can’t watch this,” he had said, and she had watched him walk out the door. She did not have the strength to be angry then. Now the anger lives under her ribs, a low hum that never turns off.

At work, she avoids the crawl spaces. That is the most obvious change. Before, she had no trouble wriggling under a house to fish new wire. Now she cannot bear the confinement—the way the dirt ceiling presses close, the memory of the MRI tube, the alien stillness of being trapped underground. She tells her boss she has back trouble. He does not argue. He probably suspects, but no one asks.

At night, the recurring dream comes: she is standing in an empty hospital corridor, and the lights are buzzing, and she knows the diagnosis is written on a clipboard in her own hand, but she cannot bring herself to read it. She wakes with her jaw clenched and her fists balled in the sheets. Sometimes she gets up at three in the morning and drives to a twenty-four-hour diner just to sit among strangers, because the quiet of her apartment feels like a waiting room.

The PCL-5 score of 46, had she known it, would not surprise her. She does not think in numbers. She thinks in small, practical observations: how she flinches when a circuit breaker snaps loud; how she has stopped making plans more than a week ahead because planning feels like tempting fate; how she cannot bring herself to schedule her annual mammogram, even though she knows it is foolish. The truth is, she is not afraid of dying anymore. She is afraid of the waiting—the long, silent stretch between tests, between heartbeats, between one safe day and the next.

She strips the last wire, twists the end into a neat hook, and reaches for the terminal screw. Her hand is steady now. She does not think about the river-cracked ceiling tile. She thinks about the light switch, the current, the simple circuit that will close when she tightens the screw.
